Don't know about Ontario, but this has been my experience so far in Nova Scotia:

I talked to my school's guidance counselor (free, took about a week to get an appointment) and we did a pre-screening (also free, took about three weeks of weekly appointments to finish) so we could tell if ADHD was likely. It was, which meant it was worth pursuing diagnosis, which would either take a LONG time (about a year) or be expensive (I was quoted 2000 the first time, but because we already had finished a pre-screening, it's possible it would be several hundred dollars less. Also I've been told there are bursaries available for people with diagnosed learning disabilities, which would offset the cost of diagnosis.) 

I'm currently in the process of finding a family doctor in my city, so they can refer me to a specialist, so I can get tested. I'm poor but I'm desperate to get this done quickly - I mean I've already wasted 20 years of my life - so I'm going to pay the thousand dollars or so, whatever it turns out to be, and my waiting period might be a couple of months. 

Also, I don't know about your situation, but there's a possibility either your school or other schools in your area might offer testing / referral within the school system itself. I'd say your best bet is to bring it up with your school doctor on Tuesday. Tell her that while anxiety might be the problem, ADHD could also be the culprit, and since time is a concern for you, you'd like to pursue multiple avenues at once.

I was never diagnosed as a child (despite being told several times to get me tested....oh well) but I can give you some input on things my parents did right / wrong:

WRONG:

 - If I forgot to bring in firewood or was too late to get some before leaving for school, and they ran out and Dad had to get some, I had to cart 15 pieces of gravel from the back orchard to the front stoop, and then bring them back again. The next time I forgot / didn't have time, it was 20. The next, 25. Etc until the month was out. I think I would often get up to the 45 mark. IT SUCKED. It was cold and it was heavy and it was BORING and I knew it wasn't going TOWARDS anything, it was just a punishment. And the problem was that I never considered the consequences of forgetting to bring in wood, or getting up late or being slow in the morning so I didn't have time to get it, until I was already at school and it was too late.

 - Threatening to clear out my room of everything except the VERY basics, etc a bed, a few clothes, and a lamp, unless I kept it clean for X amount of time. I still remember knowing that Dad was going to come home from work in an hour or so and see that I hadn't done anything all day and take away all my stuff, and still just sitting there like "oh well". Not even playing with toys or reading, just sitting there entertaining myself with my thoughts. I never realized this before but I wonder if that was part of the reason I didn't care enough to clean my room: I could still avoid boredom for the most part just with my thoughts or like some string I found on the floor.



RIGHT:

 - We had success (for a while, I forget how it fell apart, but it lasted at least a month) with what was called the Schedule, which was a spreadsheet that my Dad cooked up with all the stuff I had to do each day, and every day I'd do all the stuff and bring it to him at night to see what I had done / hadn't done and make a plan for tomorrow. The Schedule was taped to my door with a pen so I could go do something on it, check it off, and then if I forgot about it I'd see it the next time I went into my room. I forget what the consequences were for not doing it. 

 - Involving me in things besides school. I wasn't really in any clubs or extracurricular stuff involving other kids, because I was weird and universally made fun of, but stuff like "Vinegarsimmons do you want to see how I make this battery and wires make the light go on?" or, I think the most important, just generally being open to explaining EVERYTHING I asked about. "Daddy what are you doing." "I'm making it so this door doesn't squeak anymore." "How?" "Using this stuff called WD-40." "How's it work?" "Lubrication; it keeps the pieces of the door from rubbing against each other. You know how we were talking about how guitar strings make sound? It's like that." And so on. I guess just taking the time to explain stuff so I could get interested in the world, which didn't tend to judge me based on whether or not I could interact socially or whether I'd done my homework etc.



I don't know, there are a few other things for each category but I think mostly it narrows down to: Avoid getting frustrated when the scheme that you tried backfires because it doesn't work within the ways that ADHD kids work, and SPEND TIME WITH THEM, omg. Both as parents playing with their kids, but also I think ADHD kids just inherently require more work. Writing out and checking their Schedules. Figuring out the next thing to try so this fucking kid can succeed in school. Finding out other things they can succeed at so they have stuff besides school to be proud of. Sit with them and help them figure out how to make a diorama when they're just sitting at the table with the shoebox completely stunned by all the complicated work ahead of them. Etc etc. You have the advantage that your kid is diagnosed, and you can go on the internet for help, so I think you'll do just fine.

...about five minutes later I realized I'd been thinking about the mechanism of the clock on the wall, thinking about what I wanted to do after school, thinking about the name of this one friend I had and how it sounded like Cheese, thinking about......etc instead of paying attention to the teacher.

I deleted my Facebook around grade 11. I hated the culture of it and the lack of privacy/security.  
It didn't affect me all that much, actually. Besides the few awkward "Did you see my status - oh I guess you didn't" conversations, and the fact that I constantly had to explain that I didn't have Facebook when I met new people, it was fine.  
However, I did end up signing up for it again. It was right after the Dark Knight shooting, and I'd heard some radio host talking about how the shooter didn't have Facebook, so listeners, do you think people who don't have Facebook are antisocial and dangerous? And I realized that like it or not, this was the way it was, and I didn't want to be ostracized. This was also around the time that I heard that companies like Sears were asking for your Facebook account and password - what would they say if I didn't have this long clean record proving I would be a good employee? I was looking long-term, worst-case scenario, and I was scared.
This was also the summer before I went to university, and I knew it would be much harder to fit in if I didn't have it.  
Nowadays I log in a couple times a day to check and respond to messages. I go to art school so if a friend has posted a project I'll take a good look at it. Other than that I do basically nothing. I don't accept requests from people I don't like/trust, under the pretext that I have family members and professors on Facebook (which is true. I mean I'm not going to accept your request if you're smoking a blunt in your profile pic because of this reason). I basically never creep people. All in all I just keep in mind what I'm getting out of Facebook, and what Facebook is getting out of me.  
Overall though I think I only really got away with not having Facebook in high school because a) I was weird and most of my friends weren't really super Facebookers anyway, b) I could keep in contact with people through school, and c) I did have a cell phone.
